lessons.title: Project Planning and Material List
lessons.body: Before you strike an arc, you need a plan. For a small fabrication project like a steel gate, a simple table, or a charcoal stove, start by sketching the item with dimensions. Use a pencil and paperâno fancy software needed. For example, a standard gate might be 1.2 meters wide and 2 meters high. Break the project into parts: frame, bars, hinges, and latch. List each piece with its length, width, and thickness. For a gate frame, you might need 2 pieces of 40x40mm square tubing at 2m, 2 pieces at 1.2m, and 10 bars of 12mm round bar at 1.8m. Calculate total material: for square tubing, add up all lengths (2+2+1.2+1.2=6.4m) and add 10% for waste, so buy 7m. For round bar, 10 x 1.8m = 18m, buy 20m. Also list consumables: welding rods (3.2mm E6013 for general work), grinding discs, cutting discs, and paint. Check your stockâdo you have enough? If not, visit your local hardware or steel supplier. In many African markets, you can buy steel by the length or full 6m bars. Ask for a discount when buying in bulk. Also plan your time: cutting (1 hour), fit-up (1 hour), welding (2 hours), finishing (1 hour). Total about 5 hours. Write this down. A good plan saves you from running out of material halfway or wasting money on extra. Always measure twice and cut once. If youâre building for a customer, confirm the design and get a deposit for materials. This prevents loss. Remember, a clear material list is your roadmap to a successful project.

lessons.title: Cutting and Fit-Up for a Project
lessons.body: Cutting and fit-up are where accuracy begins. For cutting steel, you can use a hacksaw for small pieces, but for efficiency, use an angle grinder with a cutting disc (1mm thick for clean cuts) or a chop saw. Always wear safety glasses, gloves, and ear protection. Mark your cuts with a soapstone or marker and a try square. For a 40x40mm square tube, measure from the end and draw a line all around using a square. Clamp the tube securely before cutting. When using an angle grinder, let the tool do the workâdonât force it. For round bars, a hacksaw works fine, but a grinder is faster. After cutting, remove burrs with a grinding disc. Now fit-up: arrange the pieces on a flat surface, like a welding table or concrete floor. Use magnetic squares or clamps to hold 90-degree corners. Check diagonalsâfor a rectangular frame, measure corner to corner; both diagonals must be equal. Tack weld at corners, then recheck. For a gate, ensure the frame is square before welding fully. If youâre welding thin material, use a lower amperage (e.g., 70-90 amps for 2mm steel) to avoid burn-through. For thicker steel (5mm+), use 100-130 amps. Tack welds should be smallâabout 10mm long. After tacking, adjust if needed. Fit-up gaps should be minimal; if thereâs a gap, fill it with a small piece of metal or adjust your cut. A good fit-up means less welding and a stronger joint. Take your timeârushing here leads to a twisted project. Use a tape measure and square constantly. In Africa, where materials can be uneven, check for straightness. If a tube is bent, straighten it with a hammer or replace it. Fit-up is the foundation; get it right.

lessons.title: Welding a Small Fabrication Project
lessons.body: Now you weld. For a small project like a gate, start with tack welds at all joints. Use a 3.2mm E6013 electrode at 90-110 amps for 3mm steel. Hold the electrode at a 70-80 degree angle, dragging it along the joint. For a butt joint, use a slight back-and-forth motion to fill the gap. For T-joints, aim the arc at the corner where the two pieces meet. Keep a consistent travel speedâtoo fast gives a thin, weak weld; too slow burns through. Listen to the sound: a steady crackling like frying bacon means good settings. If it sounds like a loud hum, increase amps. Weld in short runs, about 50-75mm, then stop and let it cool slightly to prevent distortion. For a gate frame, weld the corners first, then the bars. Use a chipping hammer to remove slag after each weld, then brush with a wire brush. Inspect your welds: they should be smooth, with even ripples, and no undercut or holes. If you see holes (porosity), grind out and re-weld. For round bars, weld both sides if possible. If youâre building a charcoal stove, weld the firebox seams completely to prevent leaks. Practice on scrap first. In many African workshops, youâll use a stick welder (SMAW) because itâs affordable and works off generator or mains. If you have a MIG welder, use 0.8mm wire and 75/25 argon-CO2 gas, but stick is more common. Remember to weld in a well-ventilated areaâfumes are dangerous. After welding, let the project cool naturally. Donât quench in water unless you need to prevent warping on thin metal. A good weld is strong and neat; itâs your signature. Take pride in each bead.

lessons.title: Finishing and Cleanup
lessons.body: Finishing makes your project look professional and last longer. After welding, remove all slag, spatter, and sharp edges. Use a chipping hammer and wire brush first, then a grinding disc (4.5 inch, 60 grit) to smooth welds. For a gate or table, grind welds flush if the design calls for it, but donât over-grindâyouâll weaken the joint. Next, clean the metal with a rag and degreaser (or acetone) to remove oil and dirt. Then apply a primer. In Africa, red oxide primer is common and affordable. Brush or spray a thin, even coat. Let it dry for 2-4 hours. Then apply topcoat: enamel paint or hammered finish. For outdoor projects, use a rust-inhibiting paint. Two coats are better than one. If youâre building a charcoal stove, use high-temperature paint (black heat-resistant) on the firebox. For a gate, you might add decorative elements like scrolls or paint it black with gold accents. After painting, check for missed spots. Clean your workspace: sweep up metal shavings, put tools away, and dispose of waste properly. Sharpen your chipping hammer and replace worn grinding discs. A clean shop is a safe shop. Finally, inspect the finished project: open and close the gate, check for wobbles, ensure hinges move freely. If youâre delivering to a customer, wrap it in a blanket or cardboard to prevent scratches during transport. A good finish turns a rough fabrication into a marketable product. It shows you care about quality, which builds your reputation.

lessons.title: Portfolio and Work Sample Development
lessons.body: Your portfolio is your proof of skill. As a welder, you need to show what you can do. Start by photographing every project you completeâeven practice pieces. Use a smartphone; take clear photos from multiple angles: front, side, close-up of welds, and the finished product in use. If you donât have a phone, borrow one or ask a friend. Print the best photos (6x4 inch) and put them in a simple folder or album. Label each with the project name, date, and materials used. For example: âSteel Gate, 1.2m x 2m, made from 40x40mm square tubing and 12mm round bar, welded with E6013 rods.â Also keep a logbook of your work: list projects, hours spent, and any challenges. If you can, keep small samples: a T-joint, a butt weld, a corner joint. Clean them, paint them, and mount them on a board. This shows your bead consistency. For job applications, create a one-page resume highlighting your skills: SMAW, cutting, grinding, fit-up, blueprint reading. Include your portfolio photos. If you have a certificate, attach a copy. In Africa, many employers want to see you weld before hiring. So practice a test piece: a 6mm plate with a butt weld, a T-joint, and a lap joint. Weld them, then show them. You can also make a short video (1-2 minutes) of you welding and finishing a project. Upload to WhatsApp or YouTube if you have data. Share the link on job applications. Your portfolio is your handshakeâit speaks for you when youâre not there. Keep it updated. Even if youâre self-employed, a portfolio helps you get customers. Show it to potential clients. A strong portfolio can double your income because people trust what they can see.

lessons.title: Certification, Job Search, and Career Pathways
lessons.body: Certification proves your skills to employers and customers. In many African countries, you can get tested by a national vocational training authority, like NITA in Kenya, or similar bodies in Nigeria, South Africa, or Ghana. Look for a local welding test center. The test usually involves welding a butt joint, T-joint, and a pipe joint (if youâre going for pipe welding). Youâll be graded on bead appearance, penetration, and defects. Passing gives you a certificateâoften a Level 1, 2, or 3. Level 3 is the highest and can lead to better pay. The cost varies: in Kenya, NITA Grade 3 test might cost around 5,000 KES. Save up for it. While certified, you can also get experience through apprenticeships. Ask a local workshop if you can work as a helper. After 1-2 years, you can apply for jobs. Where to look: construction sites, welding shops, factories, and mines. In Africa, the mining and construction sectors are booming. For example, in South Africa, welders are needed in the platinum mines. In Nigeria, oil and gas companies hire pipe welders. You can also start your own businessâmake and sell gates, windows, beds, and stoves. Advertise on social media, WhatsApp groups, and local notice boards. Set fair prices: calculate material cost + labor (e.g., 30% of material cost) + profit. For a gate, if materials cost 10,000 KES, charge 15,000 KES. Reinvest in better tools: a MIG welder, a plasma cutter, or a generator. Career pathways: you can become a welding inspector, a welding instructor, or a fabrication business owner. Some welders move to offshore rigs or overseas jobs. Keep learning: take advanced courses in TIG, MIG, or pipe welding. Your career is in your handsâweld, learn, and grow.

quiz.q: What is the first step in planning a fabrication project?
options: B) Sketch the item with dimensions
quiz.explanation: Sketching with dimensions helps you visualize and plan before buying or cutting.

quiz.q: For a gate frame, you need 2 pieces of 40x40mm square tubing at 2m and 2 pieces at 1.2m. How much total length of tubing is needed?
Why should you add 10% to your material calculation?
options: A) For waste and cutting errors
C) To make the project heavier
quiz.explanation: Adding 10% accounts for waste, miscuts, and unexpected errors.

quiz.q: Which electrode is commonly used for general welding of mild steel?
quiz.explanation: E6013 is a general-purpose electrode for mild steel, easy to use.

quiz.q: What tool is best for cutting square tubing accurately and quickly?
options: B) Angle grinder with cutting disc
quiz.explanation: An angle grinder with a cutting disc is fast and accurate for metal cutting.

quiz.q: When fitting up a rectangular frame, what should you check to ensure it is square?
quiz.explanation: Measuring corner-to-corner diagonals ensures the frame is square.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for welding 2mm steel with a 3.2mm electrode?
quiz.explanation: 70-90 amps is suitable for thin steel to avoid burn-through.

quiz.q: What should you do after making a tack weld?
quiz.explanation: Always check alignment and squareness after tacking before full welding.

quiz.q: Which safety gear is essential when cutting with an angle grinder?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses and gloves protect eyes and hands from sparks and metal shards.

quiz.q: What does a steady crackling sound like frying bacon indicate during welding?
quiz.explanation: A crackling sound means the amperage is set correctly for the electrode.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a chipping hammer?
quiz.explanation: A chipping hammer is used to chip away slag after welding.

quiz.q: What defect is indicated by holes in a weld?
quiz.explanation: Porosity is the presence of gas pockets or holes in the weld.

quiz.q: Why should you weld in short runs and let the metal cool?
options: C) To make it look pretty
quiz.explanation: Short runs and cooling help prevent warping and distortion.

quiz.q: What is the first step in finishing a welded project?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning off slag and spatter is the first step before painting.

quiz.q: Which primer is commonly used in Africa for metal?
quiz.explanation: Red oxide primer is affordable and widely used for metal in Africa.

quiz.q: What type of paint should be used on a charcoal stove firebox?
quiz.explanation: High-temperature paint withstands heat without burning off.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean your workspace after finishing?
quiz.explanation: A clean workspace reduces accidents and keeps tools in good condition.

quiz.q: What should you include in a welding portfolio?
options: B) Photos of projects and a logbook
quiz.explanation: Photos and a logbook demonstrate your skills and experience.

quiz.q: How can you show your weld quality to a potential employer?
options: A) Tell them you are good
B) Show a test piece you welded
C) Show a picture of someone else's work
quiz.explanation: A physical test piece proves your actual welding ability.

quiz.q: What is a good way to advertise your welding business?
options: A) Social media and WhatsApp groups
quiz.explanation: Social media and WhatsApp are low-cost and widely used in Africa.

quiz.q: What does NITA stand for in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: NITA is the National Industrial Training Authority in Kenya, which certifies welders.

quiz.q: What is a common welding certification level in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Many vocational systems use Levels 1, 2, and 3 for welding certification.

quiz.q: Where can a certified welder find job opportunities in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Construction and mining are major employers of welders in Africa.

quiz.q: How should you price a fabricated gate?
quiz.explanation: Price should cover materials, labor, and a profit margin.

quiz.q: What is a career pathway for an experienced welder?
quiz.explanation: Welders can advance to become inspectors, instructors, or business owners.

quiz.q: What should you do with your first earnings from welding?
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting in tools improves your efficiency and income potential.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep learning after certification?
options: A) To stay competitive and learn new techniques
quiz.explanation: Continuous learning in TIG, MIG, or pipe welding opens higher-paying opportunities.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to store your welding electrodes?
quiz.explanation: Electrodes must be kept dry to prevent moisture absorption, which causes porosity.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wire brush in welding?
options: A) To clean metal before and after welding
quiz.explanation: A wire brush removes rust, dirt, and slag from the weld area.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a defect in your weld?
options: B) Grind it out and re-weld
quiz.explanation: Defects must be removed and re-welded to ensure structural integrity.
